# Markdown tables

A pipe table carries no styling of its own, so it inherits the poster body
size and the theme's rule and header treatment. This is the safe default.

| Reservoir     | Effort (h) | Catch | CPUE |
|---------------|-----------:|------:|-----:|
| Branched Oak  |       1240 |   388 | 0.31 |
| Pawnee        |        980 |   214 | 0.22 |
| Wagon Train   |       1510 |   602 | 0.40 |

Tables are drawn booktabs-style — a rule above the header, one below it, one
under the last row, and nothing else. A full grid at poster stroke weights
cages the numbers and reads as texture from three metres away.

# Tables from R

`knitr::kable()` emits a markdown pipe table for Typst output, so it lands in
the same safe path and renders identically to the one above:

```r
knitr::kable(catch, digits = 1)
```

| Species | N | Mean length (mm) |
|---------|--:|-----------------:|
| Walleye | 142 | 412.6 |
| White Bass | 318 | 268.1 |
| Channel Catfish | 96 | 501.3 |

# The HTML/CSS trap

::: {.alert title="Why this matters"}
Packages that emit **HTML** tables — `gt` among them — carry CSS sized for a
screen. Quarto's Typst writer converts `font-size: 12px` to an absolute `9pt`,
which against this poster's 27pt body is a third of the size, with no warning
at render time.

The size is only half of it: the same CSS carries the package's own colors,
borders and pixel padding. This extension drops the properties the poster
theme should be deciding — type, color, rules, spacing — so a `gt` table
renders the same as a pipe table. Alignment is kept, since that is the table's
meaning and not its decoration.

`kableExtra`'s `kbl()` is a different failure: Quarto refuses to render it to
Typst at all, before any filter runs.
:::

The table below asks for 12px and grey rules. It renders at body size in the
theme's booktabs treatment anyway.

```{=html}
<table style="font-size: 12px; border: 2px solid #D3D3D3; color: #777777;">
<thead><tr><th>Gear</th><th>Sets</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Gill net</td><td>48</td></tr>
<tr><td>Trap net</td><td>31</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

# Opting out

`table-css` under `poster:` sets how much of an HTML table's CSS is dropped:

| Value | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| `theme` | Type, color, rules and spacing come from the poster |
| `size-only` | Only the font size is dropped |
| `keep` | Nothing is dropped |

`theme` is the default and the right answer for a table you did not style on
purpose. `size-only` keeps a deliberately styled table's look at a size people
can actually read. `keep` will produce a table nobody can read from the aisle.

Per table, `typst:text:size` sizes one deliberately and exempts it from all of
this.

# Choosing a source

| Source | Emits | Safe at poster scale |
|--------|-------|----------------------|
| Pipe table | Typst table | Yes |
| `knitr::kable()` | Typst table | Yes |
| `tinytable` | Typst table | Yes |
| `gt` | HTML + CSS | Yes, with this filter |
| `kableExtra` `kbl()` | HTML | No — render fails |
| `flextable` | a raster PNG | No |

::: {.takeaway label="Rule of thumb"}
Six rows, four columns. Past that, draw it.
:::

A poster table is scanned, not studied. Anything that needs more rows than a
reader can hold in view at once belongs in a figure — or in the paper the QR
code points to.
